To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Children with brain injury have deficits in recognizing and interpreting emotions in faces and in responding to emotions in others.
children who have sustained brain injuries have difficulties in recognizing and responding appropriately to others’ emotions and that this is related to the age at the time of the injury.
emotion and empathy skills can be impaired after brain injury and that this can have a long‐term impact on social functioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of emotion‐processing skills in typically developing children, the effects of early childhood brain injury on the development of these processes, and the potential of early intervention strategies to promote the development of emotion processing skills.
understanding the nature and development of emotion‐processing skills in childhood, the impact of brain injury on these skills and the development of interventions to address deficits.
the development of emotion‐processing systems in typically developing children and adolescents, and with the effects of brain injury on the acquisition and consolidation of these skills.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a paucity of evidence on the development of emotion and emotion‐processing skills in children and adolescents after brain injury.
the development of emotion and empathic skills is an area of growing interest and research.
there is little conclusive evidence that brain injury has a specific effect on the development of emotion‐processing skills.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

emotion recognition skills are not only important to the social and emotional development of children and adolescents, but also to the social and behavioural adjustment of children who have suffered a brain injury.
emotion recognition and response skills are not static, but are subject to change throughout the lifespan.
emotion and empathy skills develop across the span of early childhood and adolescence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of emotion‐processing skills is a dynamic process that is influenced by the social and emotional environment.
there are specific phases in the development and maturation of emotion processing skills that are vulnerable to brain injury.
the ability to understand and respond to the emotions of another is a complex process that is not fully developed until the early teenage years.
